Pneumothorax

Collection of free air between the parietal and visceral pleura that causes partial or complete collapse of the lung

Potential causes of pneumothorax

Primary Spontaneous pneumothorax

Rupture of a cyst or a small sac (bleb) on the surface of the lung.

  • Young boy with no lung disease, pneumothorax after the gym → primary spontaneous pneumothorax. 441

Pneumothorax

Diagnosis is based on clinical criteria and chest x-ray

Pneumothorax

X-ray: upright inspiratory chest x-ray.

visible pleural edge with no lung markings between this edge and the chest wall

shrunken lobe or lung.

Tracheal deviation and mediastinal shift occur with large pneumothoraces.

Pneumothorax diagnosis and therapy

  • Tall, thin 20-year-old, stable, small apical pneumothorax without shift → high-flow oxygen and observation. 442 ×2

Chest tubes drainage

Tension Pneumothorax

A tension PTX is a life-threatening condition that requires immediate intervention.

Causes: penetrating chest injuries, fractures of the trachea or bronchi, a ruptured esophagus.

Progressive build-up of pressure in the pleural space pushes the mediastinum to the opposite hemithorax → obstructs venous return to the heart → circulatory instability → cardiac arrest.

Symptomes: patient is tachycardic and tachypnoeic, and may be hypoxic.

These signs are followed by circulatory collapse with hypotension and subsequent traumatic arrest with pulseless electrical activity (PEA).

Diagnosis is always clinical

Tension ptx X-ray

Deviation of the trachea away from the side of the tension.

Shift of the mediastinum.

Depression of the hemi-diaphragm

Displacement of the mediastinum and its structures (including the lung) toward the opposite side, and cause cardiopulmonary impairment (decrease cardiac output).

Tension PTX therapyDon’t forget: Life-threatening condition!

Emergent chest decompression with needle thoracostomy.

A 14-16G intravenous cannula is inserted into the second rib space in the mid-clavicular line.

The needle is advanced until air can be aspirated

into a syringe connected to the needle.

Later : Constant tube drainage

  • Trachea deviated to the LEFT, hyper-resonance and absent breath sounds on the RIGHT → needle decompression, 2nd ICS midclavicular line, RIGHT side (no CXR first). 442 ×18
  • During management of tension pneumothorax, the irrelevant step → confirming the chest tube with CT. 438

Blebectomy and pleurodesis

Added explanationSurgery (VATS bullectomy/blebectomy + pleurodesis) is offered for a second (recurrent) episode, a persistent air leak or failure to re-expand (> 3–5 days), bilateral or tension pneumothorax, or high-risk occupations (pilots, divers).
  • Second episode of pneumothorax (previous chest tube), now on a chest tube again → VATS bullectomy and pleurodesis. 439

Subcutanous Emphesema

  • Subcutaneous emphysema occurs when air is trapped under the skin.
  • It is characterized by crackling feeling on palpation of the skin known as subcutaneous crepitation which is described as touching rice krispie.
  • Both penetrating and blunt trauma to the respiratory and gastrointestinal tract can cause subcutaneous emphysema.
  • Air forced into the interstitial tissues around the pulmonary vasculature travels back toward the hilum, leading to pneumomediastinum, and this eventually tracts into the soft tissue of the neck, face, and chest wall.
  • If severe, subcutaneous emphysema can cause compression of the upper airway and jugular venous compression, which can lead to airway and cardiovascular compromise.
  • Clinically, patients can develop dysphonia and dysphagia as air dissects into the tissue planes of the neck.
  • In rare cases, where subcutaneous emphysema causes progressive dyspnea, definitive airway management with tracheostomy may be required.

Management

  • Control the source !
  • Be sure about the tube position/ holes
  • Be sure about the patency of the tube
  • Be sure about the water seal system
  • A variety of techniques to manage subcutaneous emphysema have been described in case reports.
  • bilateral 3-cm infraclavicular incisions down to pectoralis fascia.
  • using Drain / chest tube as a subcutaneous drain, then it was placed on gentle suction to ensure both tube patency and resorption of air.
  • A case report by Srinivas et al. 5 describes the use of a modified microcatheter and active compressive massage face downward and arms upward toward the catheter to facilitate drainage.

Pleural effusion

  • Accumulation of fluid between the layers of the membrane lining the lung and the chest cavity → between the partiatl and visceral pleura.
  • Pleural fluid is normally formed in small amounts to lubricate the surfaces of both pleura.
  • A pleural effusion is an abnormal collection of this fluid.

Pathophysiology of pleural effusion

  • ↑ of pulm. capill. wedge pressure: cong. heart failure
  • ↓ onc. pressure in microvas. circulation: low Se albumin
  • ↓ in pressure in the pelural space: lung collapse due to ptx
  • ↑ permeability of microvasc. circ.:due to inflam. Mediators
  • Impaired lymphatic drainage from pl. space: due to tumor / fibrosis
  • Occlusion of parietal pleura stomata with fibrin, debris and mesoth. swellings: due to inflammation, malignancy

Symptoms

  • Chest pain
    • Dyspnoe
      • Cough
    • Physical examination
      • Percussion: dull
      • Auscultation: diminished/absent breath sounds

Pleural effusion

X-ray

Small fluid: blunting of costophrenic angle

Pleural effusion

Large amount : homogenous collection

Thoracocentesis

A procedure to remove fluid in the pleural cavity

Risks: pneumothorax fluid reaccumulation, pulmonary edema,

bleeding,infection, and respiratory distress.

Pleural effusion: analysis

  • Quantity
  • Quality: color, density, opacity
  • Lab. analysis
    • Chemical
    • Cytological
    • Microbiology

TuberculosisUnilateral

Common Causes of Transudative Effusion

Congestive heart failureBilateral
CirrhosisAscites, Se protein low, usually on the right side
Nephrotic syndromeHypoproteinaemia,
Generalized oedema, ascites
  • Empyema = pus in the pleural space
    • bacteria: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pn, E. Coli, Mycobact. Tb, anaerobic bact.
    • Risk factors: alcoholism, drug use, HIV infection, neoplasm, pre-existent pulmonary disease.
    • Can be a complication of bacterial pneumonia, subdiaphragmatic abscess, esophageal perforation, following thoracic surgery

Symptoms:

  • Chest pain
    • Dyspnea
      • Cough
      • Fever
      • Night sweats
      • Weight loss

Empyema diagnosis and therapy

  • X-ray: Signs of pleural fluid
    • Ultrasonography
    • CT
    • Thoracocentesis: pus!
  • Therapy
    • prompt chest tube drainage (drainage of pleural space)
      • Antibiotics broad specturm
      • In case of uneffective therapy or recurrent empyema and pleural thickening, which may lead to functional lung impairment: surgical decortication.
  • The four possible study treatments were t-PA plus DNase, DNase plus placebo, t-PA plus placebo, and double placebo.
  • The dose of DNase was 5 mg, and the dose of t-PA was 10 mg.
  • Intrapleural medications were each given twice daily for 3 days, and each administration was followed by clamping of the drain to permit the study drug to remain in the pleural space for 1 hour.
  • Intrapleural t-PA–DNase therapy improved fluid drainage in patients with pleural infection and reduced the frequency of surgical referral and the duration of the hospital stay.

Chest Tubes

Small Bore (12-20Fr)Large Bore (24-32Fr)
  • When inserting a chest tube → full aseptic technique (no CT, no GA; adult trauma tubes are large-bore, not 12–14 Fr). 436
Speaker notes

These are just a few types of chest tube systems that there are available. It does look intimidating but I promise you they are not. Hopefully at the end of this presentation, you guys will have a better understanding and feel more comfortable working with these systems.

Indications for chest tube

Speaker notes

The body can absorb small volumes of fluid or air over time, but larger volumes limit lung expansion and cause respiratory distress. These types of situations require chest tube placement.

  • After oesophagectomy, drain fluid that turns milky white after oral intake → thoracic duct injury (chylothorax). 439 ×2

Insertion Site

Superior direction : Removal of Air (ie. Pneumothorax)

Inferior direction : Removal of Fluids (ie. Hemothorax, Empyema)

Posterior Tube Placement: Loculated (confined pocket) fluid or air → Image guided only

Speaker notes

So, when you think gravity, the heavier things are going to be found on the bottom where as air will have a tendency to float upwards.

Insertion Site → Safe Triangle

-Minimizes risk of injury to the internal mammary artery, muscle or breast tissue.

All Experts agree:

Tube placed in the midaxillary line btw 4th and 5th Ribs should successfully drain fluid or vent air

Speaker notes

Safe Triangle: an area lateral to the nipple line bordered by the latissimus dorsi, the lateral border of the pectoralis major, and the apex of the triangle below the axilla

Notes

Chest Tube Insertion Site

SAFE TRIANGLE — LANDMARKS
Anterior border: pectoralis major
Posterior border: latissimus dorsi
Inferior limit: approximately the nipple / 5th intercostal-space line
Entry point: 4th–5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line, immediately above the rib (exact space matters less than staying within the safe area)
WHY STAY WITHIN THE SAFE TRIANGLE
Improves overall procedural safety
Avoids insertion too low → risk of abdominal/diaphragmatic organ injury
Avoids unnecessary muscle trauma → less post-procedure pain
  • Haemothorax draining 1800 mL immediately → urgent thoracotomy. 442 ×3

Insertion instruments

Speaker notes

Note and review the listed components of the Simple Thoracostomy Kit .

  • Ideal chest-tube location → 4th intercostal space above the 5th rib, mid-axillary line. 439 ×9

Incise tissue to depth of rib

Carefully confirm depth and location depth

Bluntly dissect intercostal muscle

and carefully insert finger

Notes

Insertion Technique

StepKey Point
PositioningPatient lying down; prepare the whole insertion area
AnesthesiaInfiltrate local anesthetic before incision and progressively through each tissue layer — never only superficially
DissectionIncision → gradual/blunt dissection layer by layer → re-infiltrate on reaching the intercostal muscles → penetrate pleura
ConfirmationAfter entering the pleural cavity, insert a finger and confirm intrapleural position before advancing the tube
UltrasoundCan help localize the site, but finger confirmation is still required for a standard chest tube
WARNING — DIFFICULT DISSECTION
Do not aggressively dissect adhesions
If difficult or unsafe → slow down and ask for help
Significant adhesions or thick pleura may be safer managed in the OR

Insure entry into pleural cavity

and remove adhesions if present

Remove finger and monitor patient

Speaker notes

Remove finger and monitor patient for improvement or complications.

USE CAUTION. Contents in thoracic cavity MAY BE UNDER PRESSURE. Penetration into the thoracic cavity may dramatically release this pressure. Biohazard precautions and the use of personal protective equipment are necessary.

CHEST TUBE SYSTEM

Principles

3 Bottle System

Speaker notes

The concept of the 3 bottle system is what brought about the water seal chest drain system that we currently use today.

Collection Bottle and Water Seal

SUCTIONPatient

Collection Chamber: Collects drainage.

Water Seal: Maintained at 2cm, One way valve; Prevents air or fluid from returning to the chest

Notes

Chest Drain / Water-Seal System

Basic Principle

The drainage system creates a pathway for air/fluid to leave the pleural space while preventing return into the patient. Adding suction creates negative pressure throughout the system, promoting evacuation of air/fluid — fluid drainage exceeds gravity alone.

Suction Control

Tube open to Atmosphere Air

Tube To Suction

Straw under 20cmH2O

  • Suction Control: The straw submerged in the suction control bottle (typically to 20cmH2O) limits the amount of negative pressure that can be applied to the pleural space – in this case -20cmH2O
  • The submerged straw is open at the top to Atmosphere Air as the vacuum source is increased, bubbling begins in this bottle, it means atmospheric pressure is being drawn in to limit the suction level
  • The depth of the water in the suction bottle determines the amount of negative pressure that can be transmitted to the chest, NOT the reading on the vacuum regulator.
  • Higher negative pressure can increase the flow rate out of the chest, but it can also damage lung tissue
Notes

The Three-Bottle Principle

Modern chest-drain units combine three functions traditionally separated into 3 bottles/chambers:

ChamberFunction
1. CollectionClosed chamber collecting pleural fluid, primarily by gravity; separates fluid from the water-seal mechanism
2. Water SealAir from the patient passes into a tube submerged under water (~2 cm typical); air can exit but cannot flow back toward the patient
3. Suction ControlSuction applied downstream generates negative pressure throughout the system; the mechanism controlling that pressure differs between wet and dry systems (see below)
KEY RULE OF THUMB
If −20 suction is prescribed, simply dialing the wall regulator to "20" is not the key principle — it is the drainage system itself (water column or dry regulator) that determines the effective suction pressure delivered to the pleural space.

CHEST TUBE drainage Unit

Modern Day

Speaker notes

New Modern collection systems is a variation of the old 3 bottle system but with a lot more safety features

Atrium Drainage System

A: Collection Chamber

B: Water Seal

C: Suction Control

Collection Chamber

  • Fluids drain directly from patient into the collection chamber via a 6’ patient tube.
  • Fluid is calibrated in mL
  • Write on surface to note level, date & time.

Water Seal

  • Prevents air from reentering the patient
  • Intrathoracic Pressure Monitoring
  • Advance Float valve at the top of water seal: protects pt from high negativity d/t stripping or milking
  • Care:
  • Ensure 2cmH2O present in Chamber
  • Normal: “Tidaling”- Occurs with change in pressure when pt inhales and exhales
  • Abnormal: Bubbling (from R to L) – Indicates Air leak
    • Check tubing connections and pt dressing site for withdrawn catheter
    • Determine source of leak by clamping pt tube momentarily and checking to see if bubbling stops

Suction Control

Notes

Wet vs. Dry Suction

Wet SuctionDry Suction
MechanismSuction level controlled by the water column — greater depth = greater resistance = greater negative pressure requiredAdjustable wheel/valve instead of a water column
Function checkGentle bubbling confirms suction is working (excessive bubbling is not the goal)Bellows indicator shows whether suction is functioning
SettingsSet by water depthDiscrete settings, e.g. −10, −20, −30, −40 cmH₂O
NotesOlder systemLecturer's preferred system; portable versions available

Other Types…

  • Heimlich Valve (Flutter Valve):
  • One way valve, allows air to escape but keeps it from re-entering the chest cavity
  • Accommodates a small or partial pneumothorax
  • Does not collect fluid
  • Inner valve should move during exhalation
    • indicates air is flowing through the device
  • Placed in stable pts, allows for more mobility

Portable devices

Setting up the system

1. Fill the water seal chamber with 2cm of sterile water (included with chest tube set up), water will turn blue

2. Connect the patient tube to thoracic catheter

3. Set Up Suction

Water Suction: Fill chamber to 20cm,

connect the drain to vacuum, and slowly increase vacuum until gentle bubbling

appears in the suction control chamber

Dry suction: Set the dial to prescribed pressure, connect to suction source and turn to -40mmHg or higher if needed.

What information you should get

  • Check the tube if it is in place or not / kinked
  • or not ?
  • How much drainage in the last 24 hours ?
  • What is the nature of the fluid draining?
  • Is there an air leak? How much? Inspiratory / expiratory or both?
  • Look for subcutaneous emphysema?
  • Is it on suction and how much?
  • Be sure that you look to the CXR everyday ?

Assessment

USE THE ACRONYM

S = Site

T = Tubing

O = Output

P = Patency

STOP

  • S = Site
  • Check Site:
  • Ensure tube is in place.
  • No S&S of infection
  • Dressing, change q48h &
  • PRN wet or soiled (Sterile technique).
  • Subcutaneous emphysema.
  • Gunshot with a sucking chest wound, BP 70/30 → keyed three-sided dressing. 434 ×3

Subcutaneous Emphysema (Air Underneath the Skin)

Subcutaneous emphysema

(air trapped under skin)

Palpate – Crepitus (Rice Krispies)

Speaker notes

Subcutaneous Emphysema: arises as pleural space air leaks into subcutaneous tissue, when this happens tissues of the neck, face, and chest wall swell. Notify MD because tube placement or suction level may be evaluated.

STOP

  • T = Tubing
  • Connections are secured
  • No Kinks
  • Keep the drainage system below patient’s level.
  • O = Output
  • Document amount, type and color
  • Use the white write-on column on the drainage chamber to mark drainage include date & time (Check with your unit to see how often)
  • P = Patency (A: water seal)
  • Assess the water seal with the suction off
  • If water seal level is too high, it will be more difficult for air to leave the chest (aspirate water via grommet)
  • If the water seal level is too low, it leaves the water seal chamber at risk for exposure to air and can cause a pneumothorax (add sterile water via grommet)
  • P = Patency (B: Bubbling)
  • Bubbling means there is a leak in the system unless the patient has a pneumothorax.
  • Intermittent bubbling may indicate air leak from pleural space, will resolve when lung re-expands
  • Continuous bubbling suspect a leak in the system
  • Large spontaneous pneumothorax, chest tube in, lung fails to re-expand with a persistent air leak, stable → added key bronchoscopy (this year's thoracic notes: suspect an airway injury; a bigger or extra tube won't fix it). 442
  • P = Patency (C: fluctuations)
  • Normal:
    • Inspiration the water seal level will reach -10cm
    • Expiration the water seal level will reach -4cm of negative pressure normally
  • If fluctuations stop, the tubing may be obstructed (kinks, pt lying on tubing, stuck in railing, etc.)
  • If more than 2cm of water the drainage will decrease
  • If less than 2cm of water there is risk of pneumothorax

At the bedside

  • Always keep drain BELOW the chest for gravity drainage
  • Creates a pressure gradient with relatively higher pressure in the chest
  • Fluid moves from an area of higher pressure to an area of lower pressure

At the bedside – Emergency actions

Dislodged tube from patient:

  • Cover open insertion site with Vaseline gauze at peak inspiration.
  • Call for help

Dislodged from collection device

  • Clamp the tube / place the end of the tube into bottle of sterile water to create a one way valve.
  • Prepare new drainage device and connect to pt tubing

Clamping

  • Clamp Only When
  • Changing the device (the drainage system)
  • Checking for an air leak
  • Tubing is disconnected and sterile water is out of reach
  • Checking lung re-expansion prior to chest tube removal
  • DO NOT Clamp
  • Ambulating Patient
  • Transport – Disconnect suction tubing at Suction Control Stop cock.
Notes

Chest Tube Assessment on Rounds

CHECKED ROUTINELY ON EVERY ROUND
System appropriately connected — on suction or water seal?
Drainage amount, especially recent output (e.g. prior 3 h) rather than only the cumulative total
Collection level marked at a fixed time (e.g. 6 AM) to ease trend assessment
Nature/character of the fluid
Presence/absence and pattern of an air leak / bubbling
Notes

Clamping the Chest Tube

DO NOT CLAMP ROUTINELY
Routine clamping is not standard practice.
CLAMP TRIAL — KEY EXAM POINT
Used mainly when uncertain whether the patient is ready for tube removal, especially if air-leak/bubbling assessment is equivocal.
1. Clamp the chest tube
2. Wait approximately 5–6 hours
3. Obtain a chest X-ray
An ongoing air leak may show as a recurrent pneumothorax on the film — clamp + CXR helps assess readiness for removal when there is doubt.
Notes

When to Apply Suction

Suction is not routinely used — most patients stay on water seal/gravity drainage. Two recognized exceptions:

IndicationRationale
After decorticationThick pleural peel removed from a trapped lung → suction provides negative pressure to maximize re-expansion and appose the lung to the chest wall, eliminating residual pleural space (which could otherwise reaccumulate fluid)
After surgery for spontaneous pneumothorax / pleural procedureSame principle — suction keeps the lung opposed to the chest wall

Chest Tube removal

  • INDICATIONs:
  • Improved respiratory status
  • Symmetrical rise and fall of chest
  • Bilateral Breath Sounds
  • Decreased chest tube drainage
  • Absence of bubbling in the water seal chamber during inspiration
  • Improved CXR findings
  • Process:
  • Premedicate to relieve pain
  • Deep exhalation / deep inspiration (preformed before tube removal to prevent air from reentering pleural space)
  • Supplies: sterile gloves, goggles, gown, mask, dressing supplies, sterile suture removal kit, wide occlusive tape.
  • Lateral decubitus position
  • Patient performs Valsalva maneuver, chest tube removed
  • Occlusive dressing applied
  • Post CT removal CXR – ensure lung remains fully inflated
Speaker notes

Post CT removal: Monitor- Resp status, vital signs, Site for drainage, pt’s comfort level

Mastery Checklist

1 Safe triangle = pectoralis major (ant.) + latissimus dorsi (post.) + nipple/5th ICS line (inf.); enter 4th–5th ICS, mid-axillary,
above the rib.
